1.taunt: Do you count as the scrolls count, little ember?

scrolls.title: Counting from Zero
scrolls.insight: A list's first item lives at index 0, so the third item is row[2].

scrolls.title: Counting Backwards
scrolls.insight: Negative indexes count from the end: row[-1] is always the last item.

scrolls.title: The Slice Spell
scrolls.insight: A slice [a:b] starts at a and stops just before b. Strings slice too.

scrolls.title: Lists Can Change
scrolls.insight: append() adds to the end. Assigning to an index replaces that item.

questions.explanation: Indexes start at 0, so xs[1] is the second item.
questions.hint: Children count from one. Scrolls do not.

questions.explanation: xs[0] is 5 and xs[2] is 7, the first and the last.
questions.hint: Three items. Which number names the last of them?

questions.explanation: i + 1 is 2, and index 2 is the third item, 9.
questions.hint: Do the sum first. Then count the way the hollow taught you.

questions.explanation: -1 counts back from the end, so it is always the last item.
questions.hint: A minus sign does not mean nothing. It means turn around.

questions.explanation: len counts all five items. xs[-2] is second from the end: 1.
questions.hint: len() counts like a merchant. -2 walks in from the far end.

questions.explanation: xs[-1] is the last item, 4. xs[0] is the first, 1.
questions.hint: One end times the other end. Which ends?

questions.explanation: The slice starts at index 1 and stops before index 4.
questions.hint: A slice never takes the item at its last number.

questions.explanation: [:3] starts at the beginning and stops before index 3.
questions.hint: Letters line up just like list items do.

questions.explanation: append() adds one item to the end, so there are now four.
questions.hint: The list grew. len() only ever gives back a number.

questions.explanation: Assigning to xs[1] replaces the second item. Nothing is inserted.
questions.hint: Replacing is not inserting. And which one is [1]?

2.taunt: Every key knows its bucket. Do you?

scrolls.title: Keys and Values
scrolls.insight: A dict maps each key to a value. You look things up by key, not by position.

scrolls.title: The Hashing Rune
scrolls.insight: A dict hashes the key to pick a bucket, then looks only there. No searching.

scrolls.title: One Key, One Value
scrolls.insight: The same key always hashes to the same bucket, so writing it again replaces the value.

scrolls.title: Keys Must Not Change
scrolls.insight: A list can change, so its hash could not be trusted. Keys must be str, int, tuple...

scrolls.title: Asking Politely
scrolls.insight: bag["clay"] would raise KeyError. get() hands back a default instead.

questions.explanation: Looking up a key gives back its value, not the key.
questions.hint: The key opens the box. What is inside the box?

questions.explanation: Assigning to a new key adds it. len counts the keys.
questions.hint: A new key is not an error. It is a new resident.

questions.explanation: values() gives 3 and 5, and sum adds them.
questions.hint: Count what is inside, not how many boxes.

questions.explanation: The same key always hashes the same way, so it lands in the same bucket.
questions.hint: If the rune changed its mind, how would any vault find anything?

questions.explanation: x already exists, so its value is replaced in place.
questions.hint: One key. One bucket. Room for one value.

questions.explanation: Both entries share one key. The later one wins.
questions.hint: Two travellers, one bed. Who sleeps there last?

questions.explanation: clay is missing, so get() returns the default you gave it.
questions.hint: Ask politely and you are never refused. You get what you asked.

questions.explanation: in checks the keys. Only ash is there.
questions.hint: in only asks yes or no.

questions.explanation: A list can change, so it has no hash and cannot be a key.
questions.hint: What may change cannot be trusted with a bucket.

3.taunt: Round and round the kiln turns. Where does it stop?

scrolls.title: The Loop Rune
scrolls.insight: range(3) counts 0, 1, 2. It stops before the number you give it.

scrolls.title: Start, Stop, Step
scrolls.insight: range(start, stop, step) begins at start, adds step, and stops before stop.

scrolls.title: Gathering Embers
scrolls.insight: Start the total before the loop, then add to it on every pass.

scrolls.title: Loops That Wait
scrolls.insight: while repeats until its condition is False. It checks before every pass.

questions.explanation: range(4) starts at 0 and stops before 4.
questions.hint: The kiln starts cold, at nothing. And it never reaches the end.

questions.explanation: 5, 8 and 9 are greater than 4. Each adds one to count.
questions.hint: The loop visits every one. Only some pass the gate.

questions.explanation: Start at 2 and step by 2. 8 would pass the stop of 7.
questions.hint: Walk it out loud: start, add the step, check the stop.

questions.explanation: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Stop minus start is 5.
questions.hint: Ten is never reached. Count what is.

questions.explanation: A negative step counts down. It stops before reaching 0.
questions.hint: Steps may walk backwards. The stop still bars the door.

questions.explanation: 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 is 6. range(4) never gives 4.
questions.hint: List the numbers range hands out before you add a single one.

questions.explanation: Each letter is put in front of the others, so the word comes out reversed.
questions.hint: Watch which side each new letter joins.

questions.explanation: 10 becomes 6, then 2. Now 2 > 3 is False, so the loop stops.
questions.hint: Check the condition before each pass, not after.

questions.explanation: The loop stops as soon as i < 3 is False, which first happens at 3.
questions.hint: The while asks one question. When is the answer first no?
